वासुदेव परं ब्रह्म है । इन्हीं की मूर्ति परम पुरुष है, ये अव्यक्त, निर्गुण, शान्त और २५ तत्वों से परे हैं तथा अव्यय हैं, अर्थात् निर्विकार हैं ॥ १२ ॥

->प्रकृत्यन्तर्गतो देवो बहिरन्तश्च सर्वगः ।<-
->सङ्कर्षणोऽपः सृष्टवादौ तासु वीर्यमवासृजत् ॥ १३ ॥<-

शुद्धस्य ब्रह्मणो जगत्कारणत्वासम्भवादाह । प्रकृत्यन्तर्गतो मायोपहितो बहिरन्तश्च सर्वगो जगदुपादानत्वात् । एतानि सर्वाणि विशेषणानि सङ्कर्षणस्य वासुदेवांशस्यापि वासुदेवात्मकाताध्यवसानेन बोध्यानि । वासुदेवांशात्मकः सङ्कर्षणः प्रथमं जलानि निर्माय । तास्वप्सु । वीर्यं शक्तिविशेषम् । अवासृजच्चिक्षेप ॥ १३ ॥

सर्वत्र अनुभव योग्य सङ्कर्षण देव ने इसी प्रकृति के अन्तर्गत प्रविष्ट होकर सर्वप्रथम जल की रचना की । अनन्तर उस जल में बीज स्वरूप अपने तेज को स्थापित किया ॥ १३ ॥

->तदण्डमभवद् हैमं सर्वत्र तमसावृतम् ।<-
->तत्रानिरुद्धः प्रथमं व्यक्तीभूतः सनातनः ॥ १४ ॥<-

ततः किमत आह । तत् तच्छक्तिमिलितं जलं हैमं सौवर्णमण्डं गोलाकारं सर्वत्र बहिरन्तश्च अन्धकारेण आवृतमभवत् । अन्धकारसहिताकाशे सुवर्णाण्डम् अजनीत्यर्थः । तत्र सुवर्णाण्ड आदौ अनिरुद्धः सनातनौ नित्यो वसुदेवांश सङ्कर्षणोऽशरूपत्वात् व्यक्तीभूतोऽभिव्यक्तः । न तु उत्पन्नः । सत्कार्यवादाभ्युपगमात् । यथा तिलेभ्यस्तैलं सदेवाभिव्यक्तं न तु उत्पन्नम् ॥ १४ ॥

वह बीज स्वरूप तेज स्वर्ण अण्ड का रूप धारण कर लिया । वह चारों तरफ से अन्धकार से घिरा हुआ था । वहाँ (अण्ड के भीतर) सर्वप्रथम सनातन भगवान् अनिरुद्ध प्रकट हुये ॥ १४ ॥

->हिरण्यगर्भो भगवानेष छन्दसि पठ्यते ।<-
->आदित्यो ह्यदिभूतत्वात् प्रसृत्या सूर्य उच्यते ॥ १५ ॥<-

अथ अस्याभिधान्तराणि लोकसुज्ञानार्थमाह । एष सङ्कर्षणांशोऽनिरुद्ध भगवान् <term>षाइगुण्यैश्वर्य्य</term> सम्पन्नश्छन्दसि वेदे हिरण्यगर्भः सुवर्णाण्डमध्यरूपगर्भे स्थितत्वात् पठ्यते निरूप्यते । वेदेऽस्य हिरण्यगर्भ इति प्रसिद्धमभिवान्तरमित्यर्थः । हि निश्चयेन आदित्यः प्रथममभिव्यक्तत्वादुच्यते । प्रसृत्या । अस्माज्जगतोऽभिव्यक्ततयामभिनिरुद्धः सूर्य उच्यते ।

->हिरण्यगर्भः समवर्त्तताग्रे भूतस्य जातः पतिरेक आसीत् ।<-

इति श्रुतिः ॥ १५ ॥

यही भगवान् हिरण्य गर्भ हैं जिनका वेदों में उल्लेख है । सर्वप्रथम

12. Vasudeva, the supreme principle of divinity (brahman) whose form is all that is (tat), the supreme Person (purusha), unmanifested, free from qualities, superior to the twenty-five principles, imperishable,

13. Contained within matter (prakrti), divine, pervading everything, without and within, the attractor — he, having in the first place created the waters, deposited in them energy.

14. That became a golden egg, on all sides enveloped in darkness: in it first became manifested the unrestrained, the everlasting one.

15. He in the scripture (chandas) is denominated the golden-wombed (hiranyagarbha), the blessed; as being the first (Adi) existence, he is called Aditya; as being generator, the sun.

<header>Surya Siddhanta:</header>

<term>Vasudeva</term> is the Supreme Brahman. His manifestation is the Supreme Person; He is the Unmanifest, without attributes, peaceful, beyond the twenty-five <term>tattva</term> <gloss>elements</gloss>, and immutable, meaning He is without change. || 12 ||

->The Lord, who dwells within the <term>prakriti</term> <gloss>primordial nature</gloss>, is all-pervading both inside and outside.<-
-><term>Sankarshana</term> <gloss>the first expansion of the Lord</gloss>, having created the waters at the beginning of creation, cast his seed into them. || 13 ||

He explains [the verse], because the pure Brahman cannot be the cause of the world. "Dwelling within <term>prakriti</term>" means he is shrouded by <term>maya</term> <gloss>illusion</gloss>; "all-pervading inside and outside" refers to his being the material cause of the world. All these attributes should be understood as belonging to <term>Sankarshana</term>, who is an expansion of <term>Vasudeva</term>, by virtue of his oneness with <term>Vasudeva</term>. <term>Sankarshana</term>, the expansion of <term>Vasudeva</term>, first created the waters and into those waters cast his seed, a specific power. || 13 ||

The Lord <term>Sankarshana</term>, who is worthy of being experienced everywhere, entered into this <term>prakriti</term> and first created the waters. Afterward, he placed his own radiance, in the form of a seed, into those waters. || 13 ||

->That cosmic egg became golden, surrounded everywhere by darkness.<-
->Therein, the eternal <term>Aniruddha</term> was first manifested. || 14 ||

What happened next? That water, mixed with his power, became the golden egg—spherical and surrounded by darkness both inside and out. The meaning is that a golden egg was born in the sky, which was combined with darkness. Within that golden egg, the eternal <term>Aniruddha</term>—who is an expansion of <term>Vasudeva</term> and thus an aspect of him—was first manifested. He was not "born" in the ordinary sense, because we accept the doctrine that the effect pre-exists in the cause <note>referring to <term>satkaryavada</term>, the theory that the effect is an unmanifested state of the cause</note>. Just as oil is already present in sesame seeds and is merely manifested, not created. || 14 ||

That seed-like radiance assumed the form of a golden egg. It was surrounded on all sides by darkness. Within that egg, the eternal Lord <term>Aniruddha</term> first appeared. || 14 ||

->This Lord <term>Hiranyagarbha</term> <gloss>Golden Womb</gloss> is celebrated in the Vedas.<-
->He is called <term>Aditya</term> <gloss>the sun</gloss> because he is the primary being, and <term>Surya</term> because of his expansion. || 15 ||

Now, for the sake of clear understanding, he provides other names for Him. This <term>Aniruddha</term>, an expansion of <term>Sankarshana</term> who is endowed with the six qualities of divine majesty, is described in the Vedas as <term>Hiranyagarbha</term> because he resides within the golden egg. The meaning is that in the Vedas, he is famously known by this other name. He is called <term>Aditya</term> because he was the first to be manifested. He is called <term>Surya</term> because of his expansion, as he is manifested from this world. 

->"<term>Hiranyagarbha</term> existed in the beginning; he was the sole lord of all created beings."<-

This is the scriptural text. || 15 ||

ඉදම්පි ඛො මහාරාජ සන්දිට්ඨිකං සාමඤ්ඤඵලං පුරිමෙහි සන්දිට්ඨිකෙහි සාමඤ්ඤඵලෙහි අභික්කන්තතරඤ්ච පණීතතරඤ්ච.

68. පුන ච පරං මහාරාජ භික්ඛු සුඛස්ස ච පහානා දුක්ඛස්ස ච පහානා පුබ්බෙව සොමනස්සදොමනස්සානං අත්ථඞ්ගමා අදුක්ඛමසුඛං උපෙක්ඛාසතිපාරිසුද්ධිං චතුත්ථං ඣානං උපසම්පජ්ජ විහරති. සො ඉමමෙව කායං පරිසුද්ධෙන චෙතසා පරියොදාතෙන ඵරිත්වා නිසින්නො හොති. නාස්ස කිඤ්චි සබ්බාවතො කායස්ස පරිසුද්ධෙන චෙතසා පරියොදාතෙන අප්ඵුටං හොති.

සෙය්‍යථාපි මහාරාජ පුරිසො ඔදතෙන වත්ථෙන සබ්බං පාරුපිතවා නිසින්නො අස්ස, නාස්ස කිඤ්චි සබ්බාවතො කායස්ස ඔදතෙන වත්ථෙන අප්ඵුටං අස්ස, එවමෙව ඛො මහාරාජ භික්ඛු ඉමමෙව කායං පරිසුද්ධෙන චෙතසා පරියොදාතෙන ඵරිත්වා නිසින්නො හොති. නාස්ස කිඤ්චි සබ්බාවතො කායස්ස පරිසුද්ධෙන චෙතසා පරියොදාතෙන අප්ඵුටං හොති.

ඉදම්පි ඛො මහාරාජ සන්දිට්ඨිකං සාමඤ්ඤඵලං පුරිමෙහි සන්දිට්ඨිකෙහි සාමඤ්ඤඵලෙහි අභික්කන්තතරඤ්ච පණීතතරඤ්ච.

69. පුන ච පරං මහාරාජ සො භික්ඛු එවං සමාහිතෙ චිත්තෙ පරිසුද්ධෙ පරියොදාතෙ අනඞ්ගණෙ විගතූපක්කිලෙසෙ මුදුභූතෙ කම්මනීයෙ ඨිතෙ ආනෙඞ්ජප්පත්තාය චිත්තං අභිනය්‍යති අභිහරිති. සො එවං පජානාති: “අයං ඛො මෙ කායො රූපී චාතුම්මහාභූතිකො මාතාපෙත්තිකසම්භවො ඔදනකුම්මාසුපචයො අනිච්චුච්ඡාදනපරිමද්දන-භෙදනවිද්ධංසනධම්මො. ඉදඤ්ච පන මෙ විඤ්ඤාණං එත්ථ සිතං එත්ථ පටිබද්ධ”න්ති.

4.3.2.6. Second Absorption
Furthermore, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, a mendicant enters and remains in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.
They drench, steep, fill, and spread themselves with rapture and bliss born of immersion. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with rapture and bliss born of immersion.
It’s like a deep lake fed by spring water. There’s no inlet to the east, west, north, or south, and the heavens would not properly bestow showers from time to time.
But the stream of cool water welling up in the lake drenches, steeps, fills, and spreads throughout the lake. There’s no part of the lake that’s not spread through with cool water.
In the same way, a mendicant drenches, steeps, fills, and spreads themselves with rapture and bliss born of immersion. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with rapture and bliss born of immersion.
This too, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life that’s apparent in the present life which is better and finer than the former ones.
4.3.2.7. Third Absorption
Furthermore, with the fading away of rapture, a mendicant enters and remains in the third absorption, where they meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’
They drench, steep, fill, and spread themselves with bliss free of rapture. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with bliss free of rapture.
It’s like a pool with blue water lilies, or pink or white lotuses. Some of them sprout and grow in the water without rising above it, thriving underwater. From the tip to the root they’re drenched, steeped, filled, and soaked with cool water. There’s no part of them that’s not soaked with cool water.
In the same way, a mendicant drenches, steeps, fills, and spreads themselves with bliss free of rapture. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with bliss free of rapture.
This too, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life that’s apparent in the present life which is better and finer than the former ones.
4.3.2.8. Fourth Absorption
Furthermore, with the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, a mendicant enters and remains in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.
They sit spreading their body through with pure bright mind. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with pure bright mind.
It’s like someone sitting wrapped from head to foot with white cloth. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread over with white cloth.
In the same way, they sit spreading their body through with pure bright mind. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with pure bright mind.
This too, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life that’s apparent in the present life which is better and finer than the former ones.
4.3.3. The Eight Knowledges
4.3.3.1. Knowledge and Vision
When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they project it and extend it toward knowledge and vision.
They understand:
‘This body of mine is formed. It’s made up of the four principal states, produced by mother and father, built up from rice and porridge, liable to impermanence, to wearing away and erosion, to breaking up and destruction.
And this consciousness of mine is attached to it, tied to it.’
Suppose there was a beryl gem that was naturally lustrous, eight-faceted, well-worked, transparent, clear, and unclouded, endowed with all good qualities.
And it was strung with a thread of blue, yellow, red, white, or golden brown.
And a person with clear eyes were to take it in their hand and examine it:
‘This beryl gem is naturally lustrous, eight-faceted, well-worked, transparent, clear, and unclouded, endowed with all good qualities.
And it’s strung with a thread of blue, yellow, red, white, or golden brown.’
In the same way, when their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they project it and extend it toward knowledge and vision.
This too, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life that’s apparent in the present life which is better and finer than the former ones.
4.3.3.2. Mind-Made Body
When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they project it and extend it toward the creation of a mind-made body.
From this body they create another body—formed, mind-made, whole in its major and minor limbs, not deficient in any faculty.
Suppose a person was to draw a reed out from its sheath.
They’d think:
‘This is the reed, this is the sheath. The reed and the sheath are different things. The reed has been drawn out from the sheath.’
Or suppose a person was to draw a sword out from its scabbard.
They’d think:
‘This is the sword, this is the scabbard. The sword and the scabbard are different things. The sword has been drawn out from the scabbard.’
Or suppose a person was to draw a snake out from its slough.
They’d think:
‘This is the snake, this is the slough. The snake and the slough are different things. The snake has been drawn out from the slough.’
In the same way, when their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they project it and extend it toward the creation of a mind-made body.
From this body they create another body—formed, mind-made, whole in its major and minor limbs, not deficient in any faculty.
This too, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life that’s apparent in the present life which is better and finer than the former ones.
4.3.3.3. Psychic Powers
When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they project it and extend it toward psychic power.
They wield the many kinds of psychic power: multiplying themselves and becoming one again; materializing and dematerializing; going unobstructed through a wall, a rampart, or a mountain as if through space; diving in and out of the earth as if it were water; walking on water as if it were earth; flying cross-legged through the sky like a bird; touching and stroking with the hand the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; controlling the body as far as the realm of divinity.
Suppose a deft potter or their apprentice had some well-prepared clay. They could produce any kind of pot that they like.
Or suppose a deft ivory-carver or their apprentice had some well-prepared ivory. They could produce any kind of ivory item that they like.
Or suppose a deft goldsmith or their apprentice had some well-prepared gold. They could produce any kind of gold item that they like.
In the same way, when their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they project it and extend it toward psychic power.
This too, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life that’s apparent in the present life which is better and finer than the former ones.
4.3.3.4. Clairaudience
When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they project it and extend it toward clairaudience.
With clairaudience that is purified and superhuman, they hear both kinds of sounds, human and heavenly, whether near or far.
Suppose there was a person traveling along the road. They’d hear the sound of drums, clay drums, horns, kettledrums, and tom-toms. They’d think: ‘That’s the sound of drums,’ and ‘that’s the sound of clay drums,’ and ‘that’s the sound of horns, kettledrums, and tom-toms.’
In the same way, when their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they project it and extend it toward clairaudience.

## From that comes speed of mind, independence of the senses <note>original: "vikaraṇa-bhāva"</note>, and mastery over the primal source. ॥ 48 ॥

Speed of mind is the attainment of incomparable movement for the body. Independence of the senses is the attainment of the activity of the senses, whether they are separated from the body <note>original: "videha"</note> or not, dependent upon the desired place, time, and object. Mastery over the primal source is the control over all the modifications of the primary matter <term>prakṛti</term> <gloss>the fundamental creative force</gloss>. These three accomplishments are called "honey-like" <note>original: "madhu-pratīkā"</note>. They are attained through the mastery of the five forms of the sense-organs. ॥ 48 ॥

## For one established only in the discernment between the pure intellect <term>sattva</term> and the Self <term>puruṣa</term>, there arises lordship over all states and omniscience. ॥ 49 ॥

For one who is abiding in the highest clarity of the pure intellect <term>buddhi-sattva</term>, cleansed of the impurities of activity <term>rajas</term> and inertia <term>tamas</term>, and who is currently in the state known as the "highest mastery," there arises lordship over all states, established solely in the discernment between the pure intellect and the Self. All beings are qualities <term>guṇas</term>, which are essentially business and...

He speaks of the accomplishments arising from the mastery of the five forms of the senses: **"From that comes speed of mind, independence of the senses, and mastery over the primal source."** The sense-organ's condition when separated from the body is the "independence of the senses." "Place" means places like Kashmir. "Time" means past time and the rest. "Object" means subtle objects and the rest. Following that, mastery over the primal source is control over all modifications of the primary matter. These accomplishments are called "honey-like" by those learned in the science of yoga. 

One might ask: even if the senses with their objects are mastered through mastery of the senses, what is the consequence regarding the primary source <term>pradhāna</term> and its causes? To this, he says: **"And these..."** Through mastery of the five forms of the sense-organs, such as apprehension. This means: these accomplishments are not merely from mastery of the sense-organ itself, but of its five forms, and included within that is the primary source and its derivatives. ॥ 48 ॥

He shows the secondary powers <term>vibhūti</term> of that discernment between the pure intellect and the Self—which is the goal of those <term>saṃyamas</term> that are the causes of power in the form of knowledge and action—by showing it to be the fruit of the faith accomplished by one's own mastery: **"For one established only in the discernment between the pure intellect and the Self, there arises lordship over all states and omniscience."** "Clarity" comes from the removal of the impurities of activity and inertia. From that comes the "highest state of mastery." For the mind-stuff <term>citta-sattva</term> was certainly subservient when clouded by activity and inertia. But upon their cessation, when it is subservient to the yogi who has mastery, there arises in that yogi, who is established solely in the discernment between the pure intellect and the Self, lordship over all states. He clarifies this: **"All beings are..."**

48. As a result of this [there follows] speed [great as that] of the central-organ, action of the instruments of [knowledge] disjunct [from the body], and the subjugation of the primary-cause.

Speed of the mind means that the body acquires motion comparable [to that] of the mind. Action of the instruments of knowledge disjunct [from the body] is the acquisition by the discarnate organs of the fluctuation required for the place and time and object desired. Subjugation of the primary cause is the mastery over all evolving causes and evolved effects. These three perfections are called Honey-Faced (rnadhupratika). And they are acquired as the result of the subjugation in five forms of instruments [of perception].

He describes the perfections which result from the subjugation, in five kinds, of the organs. 48. As a result of this .... and the subjugation. The fact that the organs are instruments [of perception] even for the discarnate is described as being the action of the instruments [of perception] disjunct [from the body].

The place is Kashmir or some other [place]. The time is the past or some other [time]. The object is subtile or other. As a result of the subjugation of the organ and of the inherence, [there follows] mastery of all evolving-causes and evolved-effects, a subjugation of the primary cause. These perfections are called Honey- Faced by those persons who are expert in the yoga system. An objector says 'This may be true. By subjugation of the organs, the organs together with their objects may be mastered. But what is gained [by subjugation] of the primary cause and the other causes of these [organs] ? ' In reply to this he says «And they.» The instruments [of perception] are the organs. The five forms are [the five] processes-of-knowing [iii. 47]. [The result follows] from the subjugation of these. What he means to say is this : These perfections are not- a result of a subjugation of organs in general but of the five forms [of the processes-of-knowing]. And included in these [five] is the primary-cause and the rest.

49. He who has only the full discernment into the difference between the sattva and the Self is one who has authority over all states-of-existence and is one who knows all.

He who is grounded in only the full discernment into the difference between the sattva and the Self, and who is in the higher consciousness of being master in the higher clearness, and who has the sattva of his thinking-substance cleansed from the defilement of rajas and tamas is one who has authority over all states-of-existence. The aspects (guna) which are the essence of all things, which have both the determinations and the objects-of-determinations as their essence, present themselves as being the essence of the object-for-sight in its totality to their Owner, the Soul (ksetrajna). This is the meaning. — Being <one who knows alb refers to the [intuitive] knowledge, produced by discrimination and rising instantaneously [into consciousness], of the aspects (guna) which are the essence of all, whether they be [iii. 14] quiescent or uprisen or indeterminable. This is the meaning. It is this perfection that is termed [i. 36] the ' undistressed,' by attaining to which the yogin who knows all, whose hindrances and bondages have dwindled, takes his recreation as having mastery.

These same constraints, Which whether mediately or immediately lead to powers in the form of knowledge and of activity, are for the sake of the discernment into the difference between the sattva and the Self by way of the confidence produced by grasping the perfections in turn and binding them together. The supernormal powers subsidiary to this [discernment] are shown [in the sutra]. 49. Sattva . . . and. There is clearness in so far as the defilement by rajas and tamas has been washed away. As a result of this there is the higher consciousness of being master. It was inevitable that the sattva of the mind-stuff should be overwhelmed by the rajas and tamas. But when the latter subside, it is this [sattva] that is to be mastered by the yogin its master. When it is mastered, the yogin who is grounded in only the full discernment of the difference between the sattva and the Self, is one who has authority over all states-of-existence. This same he explains by the words «essence of all things.»

No purpose is seen or heard when the others are understood as superior. However, when the Person <term>Purusha</term> <gloss>the Supreme Being</gloss>—who is higher than the senses and so on, and beyond the whole range of worldly objects—is understood, a purpose is seen: the attainment of liberation <term>moksha</term> <gloss>freedom from the cycle of rebirth</gloss>. Thus says the Scripture <term>Shruti</term> <gloss>revealed text</gloss>: "By perceiving That, one is released from the jaws of death" <note>quoting Katha Upanishad 3.15</note>. 

Furthermore, by the denial of anything higher and by the use of the word "limit" <term>kastha</term> <gloss>the highest point or goal</gloss>, the text shows its focus on the Person. It shows that the preceding and succeeding flow of descriptions is solely for the purpose of understanding the Person. Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of the narrative" <note>original: "akhyanaya"</note>: it means for the purpose of the perfect knowledge <term>samyag-darshana</term> <gloss>true spiritual realization</gloss> that is preceded by the narrative. Indeed, this narrative is taught for the sake of perfect knowledge, and the narrative itself is not the primary subject. (14)

### And because of the word "Self". (3.3.15)

For this reason also, the description of the sequence starting from the senses is intended only for the realization of the Person. This is because the text refers to the Person under discussion as the Self <term>Atman</term> <gloss>the innermost essence</gloss>, saying: "This Self is hidden in all beings and does not shine forth; but it is seen by subtle seers through their sharp and subtle intellect" <note>quoting Katha Upanishad 3.12</note>. From this, it is understood that the quality of being the Self is not intended for the other things mentioned. The text further shows that it is difficult to know and can only be reached by a refined intellect. For the sake of knowing That, it prescribes the following practice: "The wise man should restrain speech in the mind" <note>quoting Katha Upanishad 3.13</note>. **The Splendor of the Commentary**
<note>Sub-commentary by Vachaspati Mishra</note>
The Veda, by using the sign of denying anything higher with the phrase "That is the limit," shows that the focus is on the Person. It shows that the statements of superiority of one thing over another are for that purpose. For the objects and so on, their superiority is taught as a prelude to the narrative, solely to lead to the vision of the Person, as they have no purpose of their own. (14) Regarding "And because of the word Self": Since there is consistency between the beginning and the end in phrases like "That is the supreme step of Vishnu" and "Nothing is higher than the Person," it is determined that there is a single sentence <term>ekavakyatva</term> <gloss>thematic unity</gloss> focused on the one Person. It is not proper to imagine a split in the sentence or a split in the results, as that would be overly complex. (15)

**The Determination of Justice**
<note>Sub-commentary by Anandagiri</note>
Regarding the question "Why?": The author thinks that because the others lack a goal or result, they should not be the primary objects of knowledge. He asks how there can be an absence of purpose. He considers whether the result is established by logic or scripture and denies the first by saying "no." To the second, he says "nor is it heard." Because this context is seen to concern the nature of reality, it cannot be about the rules of worship. Since it is possible for it to concern the knowledge of the Supreme Goal, it is not reasonable to claim it concerns the senses or other things. If it is asked how the knowledge of the Person as superior leads to the human goal, he says that because the Person is the infinite object beyond all voidness, the realization of the Person's superiority is experienced as indestructible. Since the removal of ignorance and false knowledge is a visible result, it is not right to imagine an unseen one. For those who disagree, he cites the scripture: "Thus it is." He further says this entire context has the realization of the Person as its total focus. By the sign of denial "Higher than the Person [there is nothing]" and the word "limit," the Veda shows its regard for the Person. The "flow of the preceding and succeeding" refers to the statements of one being higher than the other. Since there is no command for meditation here, he explains the part of the sutra: "For the purpose of the narrative." Even the knowledge of the attributeless Brahman serves the goal because Brahman is the ground. He explains the reason why only the Person is the subject: "And because of the word Self." (14) He clarifies the term "Self" from the sutra. He dismisses the doubt that the Self's non-shining is natural by quoting "but it is seen." He refers to the Person under discussion. He notes the difficulty of knowing it and the need for a refined mind. He mentions the other reason indicated by the word "and" in the sutra. The control of speech and so on is seen in the verse, but it is not a rule for meditation. Because the Self is difficult to know from scripture and tradition, and the senses are easy to know, the statement of their superiority is only to point towards the intended goal. (15)

To this we reply as follows.

We must assume that the whole passage aims at intimating only that the person is higher than everything. Any information as to the relative superiority of the preceding members of the series would be devoid of all purpose ; for of the knowledge derived from such observation a use is neither to be seen nor declared by scripture. Of the knowledge, on the other hand, of the person being higher than the senses and everything else, raised above all evil, we do see a purpose, viz. the accomplishment of final release. And so scripture also says, ' He who has perceived that is freed from the jaws of death' (I, 3, 15). Moreover, the text by declaring that nothing is higher than the person and that he is the highest goal intimates reverence for the person, and thereby shows that the whole series of objects is enumerated only to the end of giving information about the person. — ' For the purpose of pious meditation,' i.e. for the purpose of perfect knowledge which has pious meditation for its antecedent. For the passage under consideration does not teach pious meditation by itself.

15. And on account of the word ' Self.'

The above conclusion is confirmed by the circumstance that the person under discussion is called the Self in I, 3, 12, 'That Self is hidden in all beings and does not shine forth, but it is seen by subtle seers through their sharp and subtle intellect.' From this we conclude that the text wishes to represent the other beings enumerated as the Non-Self. The passage quoted, moreover, indicates that the person is hard to know, and to be reached by sharp minds only. — Again, the passage (I, 3, 13), 'A wise man should keep down speech and mind,' enjoins pious meditation as a means of the knowledge of the highest person, as we have explained under I, 4, i. — It thus follows that scripture indicates various excellences in the case of the purusha only, and not in that of the other beings enumerated.— The passage, moreover, ' He reaches the end of his journey and that is the highest place of Vish/m,' suggests the question as to who is the end of the journey and so on, and we therefore conclude that the enumeration of the senses, objects, &c., has merely the purpose of teaching the highest place of Vish;/u (not of teaching anything about the relation of the senses, objects, and so on).
